{{nihongo|'''Kiiti Morita'''|森田 紀一|Morita Kiichi|February 11, 1915 &ndash; August 4, 1995}} was a Japanese [[mathematician]] working in [[algebra]] and [[topology]].

Morita was born in 1915 in [[Hamamatsu]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]] and graduated from the [[University of Tsukuba|Tokyo Higher Normal School]] in 1936. Three years later he was appointed assistant at the [[Tokyo University of Science]].<ref name="notices"/> He received his Ph.D. from [[Osaka Prefecture University|Osaka University]] in 1950, with a thesis in topology.<ref name="notices">{{cite journal | last1 = Arhangelskii | first1 = A.V. |author-link=Alexander Arhangelskii | last2 = Goodearl | first2 = K.R. | last3 = Huisgen-Zimmermann | first3 = B.| title = Kiiti Morita 1915-1995 | journal = [[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume = 44 | issue = 6 | pages = 680–684 | publisher = American Mathematical Society | location = Providence, RI | date = June–July 1997 | url = https://www.ams.org/notices/199706/morita.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=30034}}</ref> After teaching at the Tokyo Higher Normal School, he became professor at the [[University of Tsukuba]] in 1951. He held this position until 1978, after which he taught at [[Sophia University]].<ref name="notices"/><ref name="nyt"/> Morita died of heart failure in 1995 at the Sakakibara Heart Institute in [[Tokyo]];<ref name="nyt">{{cite web|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=990CEEDE1E38F936A35753C1A963958260|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| title=Obituary: Kiiti Morita, Mathematician, 80|date=October 5, 1995|access-date=July 23, 2020}}</ref> he was survived by his wife, Tomiko, his son, Yasuhiro, and a grandson.<ref name="nyt"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/development/mor-jhe.html|title= Memorial address by John Ewing|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|date=August 4, 1998|access-date=July 23, 2020}}</ref>

He introduced the concepts now known as [[Morita equivalence]] and [[Morita duality]] which were given wide circulation in the 1960s by [[Hyman Bass]] in a series of lectures. The [[Morita conjectures]] on [[normal space|normal topological spaces]] are also named after him.
